ko.title: DHS, 난민 지위 종료 통지 응답 기간 30일에서 10일로 단축
ko.summary: 국토안보부(DHS)가 8 CFR Part 207을 개정하는 잠정 최종규칙(interim final rule)을 발표해, 난민 지위 종료 의향 통지(NOIT)에 대한 응답 기간을 기존 30일에서 10일로 단축했습니다. 이 규칙은 연방관보(Federal Register)에 게재되는 즉시 효력이 발생하며, 동시에 공개 의견 수렴 절차도 진행됩니다.
points: USCIS가 이미 난민으로 입국을 허가받은 사람에게 발급하는 종료 의향 통지(NOIT)에 대한 응답 기간이 30일에서 10일로 줄어듭니다.
이번 조치는 연방관보 게재일에 즉시 효력이 발생하는 잠정 최종규칙 형태이며, 최종 확정된 규칙은 아니고 의견 수렴 후 변경될 수 있습니다.
의견 제출 기한은 연방관보 게재일로부터 30일이며, 정확한 날짜는 게재 시점에 확정되므로 원문에는 구체적 날짜가 명시되어 있지 않습니다.
의견은 regulations.gov를 통해 DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397을 참조해 영어로 제출해야 합니다.
DHS는 전임 행정부 시기 난민 심사 절차가 완화되어 신원 확인이 부실했던 사례와 사기 위험을 규칙 제정 근거로 제시했습니다.
난민 지위 자격 요건 자체는 변경되지 않으며, 지위 종료 절차의 응답 기간만 단축됩니다.
ko.who: 이미 난민 지위로 미국에 입국했으며 향후 지위 종료 의향 통지를 받을 수 있는 사람들과 이들을 대리하는 변호사에게 영향을 미칩니다.
ko.action: 관련 당사자와 변호사는 종료 의향 통지를 받을 경우 단축된 10일 이내에 대응할 준비를 해야 하며, 이해관계자는 게재일로부터 30일 이내에 regulations.gov를 통해 의견을 제출할 수 있습니다.

en.title: DHS Cuts Refugee Status Termination Notice Response Time From 30 to 10 Days
en.summary: DHS has issued an interim final rule amending 8 CFR Part 207 to shorten the response window for a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) refugee status from 30 days to 10 days. The rule becomes effective upon publication in the Federal Register, while also remaining open for public comment.
points: The response period for a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) refugee status is reduced from 30 days to 10 days.
This is an interim final rule, effective on the date it is published in the Federal Register, not yet a final, settled rule.
Public comments are due 30 days after the publication date; the exact calendar date is not specified in the source text.
Comments must be submitted in English through regulations.gov, referencing DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397.
DHS cites concerns about weakened vetting during a prior administration and related fraud investigations as justification for the change.
The underlying eligibility criteria for refugee status are not changed, only the timeline for responding to a termination notice.
en.who: People already admitted to the United States as refugees who may receive a termination notice, and their attorneys.
en.action: Affected individuals and their attorneys should be prepared to respond to any Notice of Intent to Terminate within the new 10 day window, and interested parties may submit comments via regulations.gov within 30 days of publication.

es.title: DHS reduce de 30 a 10 días el plazo para responder al aviso de terminación de refugio
es.summary: El Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) emitió una regla final provisional que modifica el 8 CFR Part 207 para reducir de 30 a 10 días el plazo de respuesta al Aviso de Intención de Terminar (NOIT) el estatus de refugiado. La regla entra en vigor el día de su publicación en el Federal Register y, a la vez, queda abierta a comentarios públicos.
points: El plazo para responder a un Aviso de Intención de Terminar (NOIT) el estatus de refugiado se reduce de 30 a 10 días.
Se trata de una regla final provisional, vigente desde la fecha de publicación en el Federal Register, no es una regla definitiva.
Los comentarios públicos deben presentarse dentro de los 30 días posteriores a la publicación; la fuente no indica la fecha exacta.
Los comentarios deben enviarse en inglés a través de regulations.gov, citando el expediente DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397.
DHS justifica el cambio señalando procedimientos de verificación debilitados durante la administración anterior e investigaciones de fraude relacionadas.
Los criterios de elegibilidad para el estatus de refugiado no cambian, solo el plazo de respuesta al aviso de terminación.
es.who: Personas ya admitidas en Estados Unidos como refugiados que podrían recibir un aviso de terminación de estatus, y sus abogados.
es.action: Las personas afectadas y sus abogados deben estar preparados para responder a cualquier Aviso de Intención de Terminar dentro del nuevo plazo de 10 días, y las partes interesadas pueden enviar comentarios a través de regulations.gov dentro de los 30 días posteriores a la publicación.

zh.title: DHS将难民身份终止通知的回应期从30天缩短至10天
zh.summary: 美国国土安全部(DHS)发布一项临时最终规则,修订8 CFR Part 207,将难民身份终止意向通知(NOIT)的回应期限从30天缩短为10天。该规则自在《联邦公报》刊登之日起生效,同时仍接受公众意见。
points: 难民身份终止意向通知(NOIT)的回应期限从30天缩短为10天。
这是一项临时最终规则,自《联邦公报》刊登之日起生效,尚非最终确定的规则。
公众意见须在刊登日起30天内提交,原文未给出具体截止日期。
意见须以英文通过regulations.gov提交,并注明DHS案卷编号USCIS-2026-0397。
DHS表示,此前一届政府时期的难民审查程序把关不严,并存在相关欺诈调查案例,是此次修规的依据。
难民身份的资格认定标准本身未改变,只是缩短了对终止通知的回应时限。
zh.who: 已以难民身份获准入境美国、可能收到身份终止通知的人士及其代理律师。
zh.action: 受影响人士及其律师应为可能收到的终止意向通知做好准备,在新的10天期限内及时回应,利益相关方可在刊登之日起30天内通过regulations.gov提交意见。

ja.title: DHS、難民資格取消通知への回答期限を30日から10日に短縮
ja.summary: 米国土安全保障省(DHS)は8 CFR Part 207を改正する暫定最終規則を発表し、難民資格の取消意向通知(NOIT)に対する回答期限を30日から10日へ短縮しました。本規則は連邦官報に掲載された日から発効する一方、意見公募も行われます。
points: 難民資格の取消意向通知(NOIT)への回答期限が30日から10日に短縮されます。
本規則は暫定最終規則であり、連邦官報掲載日に発効しますが、まだ最終確定したものではありません。
意見提出期限は掲載日から30日以内とされていますが、原文には具体的な日付は記載されていません。
意見はregulations.govを通じて英語で提出し、DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397を明記する必要があります。
DHSは前政権下で難民審査手続きが緩められ、不正リスクが高まったとされる調査事例を改正の根拠として挙げています。
難民資格そのものの認定基準は変更されず、取消手続きにおける回答期限のみが短縮されます。
ja.who: 既に難民として米国に入国しており、今後取消意向通知を受け取る可能性がある人、およびその代理弁護士。
ja.action: 対象者とその弁護士は、取消意向通知を受け取った場合に新たな10日以内の期限で対応できるよう準備し、関係者は掲載日から30日以内にregulations.govを通じて意見を提出することができます。

ACTION: Interim final rule.

SUMMARY: This interim final rule (IFR) amends Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations to expedite termination of refugee status when DHS determines an alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time of admission to the United States. The response period to a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) is reduced from thirty to ten days. These changes aim to restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and exploitation.

II. Executive Summary A. Purpose of the Regulatory Action The purpose of this rulemaking is to shorten the termination notice period in order to mitigate potential risks posed by aliens admitted to the United States as refugees when, in fact, they were not eligible for refugee classification at the time of admission. Those who are improperly admitted may not have their identity fully confirmed and vetted due to an incomplete record, and as such pose a risk to program integrity and may pose a risk to national security and public safety. A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records.1 Operational guidance implemented during this period allowed officers to forgo typical lines of inquiry, sacrificing the caliber and efficacy of the refugee interview, a critical screening component of the refugee adjudication process.2 The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews. Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the 1 Refugee applicants have the burden to establish their identity for purposes of immigration benefits. Identity is a critical element in refugee adjudications because it helps verify that the applicant is who they say they are. Identity can be established through the collection of biometrics, documentary evidence, and testimony. In the refugee context, testimony is a primary source of evidence. It provides valuable information about the applicant’s background, familial relations, past experiences, and associations which provide context in establishing who the applicant is as a person and whether they are eligible for the benefit sought. An applicant’s capacity to demonstrate their identity to the satisfaction of the U.S. Government, ensuring that officials are confident in the applicant’s identity, is a necessary step in determining eligibility for the immigration benefit requested.

2 Cases of resettled refugees residing in Minnesota were reviewed as part of an initial pilot operation cohort to reinforce recent joint antifraud enforcement actions, such as Operation Twin Shield, conducted with other law enforcement partners including ICE and the FBI.

United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States. This is supported by a recent preliminary review of admitted refugees residing in Minnesota who were interviewed, approved, and admitted during the Biden administration. For the majority of these reviewed cases, the evidence was insufficient to establish that the principal applicant met all of the required elements of the refugee definition.3 The goal was to have as many refugees as practicable enter the United States to meet President Biden’s ceiling for refugee admissions and in order to accomplish this, a number of requirements for ensuring a thorough examination and assessment of eligibility were reduced or removed.

This raises concerns about the integrity of the refugee program and calls into question the eligibility for refugee status of aliens admitted to the United States during this time. As detailed below in this preamble, several policy decisions were implemented that significantly reduced the integrity measures within the refugee program. These changes resulted in an increase in the number of refugee interviews conducted per officer each day, with less comprehensive elicitation of testimony from applicants. These adjustments limited the ability of refugee officers, and the U.S. government to accurately determine whether an applicant’s identity was properly established, assess potential national security or public safety concerns, and verify whether the applicant met the definition of a refugee.

To protect U.S. interests and public safety, USCIS must act swiftly when DHS determines that an alien did not meet the refugee definition and was not entitled to refugee status at the time of admission. Shortening the NOIT response period enables DHS to respond rapidly to such findings. Allowing a longer notice period could provide 3 See USCIS Announces Results of Operation Twin Shield, a Large-Scale Immigration Fraud Investigation (Sept. 30, 2025), https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/news-releases/uscis-announces-results-of-operation- twin-shield-a-large-scale-immigration-fraud-investigation.

opportunities for aliens to evade enforcement or engage in harmful activities. For example, the Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) Directorate investigated cases where refugees were later identified as members of armed groups or had concealed extremist affiliations. In one case, a refugee was found to have participated in human rights abuses with the Liberian Armed Forces during the Liberian Civil War. In another case, a refugee was found to have misrepresented his involvement with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), an armed group in Ethiopia. Social media checks indicated numerous pro-OLF activities and pro-OLF and radical violent rhetoric posted prior to his admission to the United States as a refugee. These cases demonstrate that when credible evidence of national security or public safety concerns arises after a refugee’s admission, USCIS may be unable to initiate removal proceedings until the termination process is complete. Therefore, reducing the response period to ten days after issuance of a NOIT allows USCIS to address such threats more quickly and effectively, restoring integrity to the immigration system.

To be eligible for admission to the United States as a refugee, an alien must establish, among other things, that they meet the definition of “refugee” as defined in section 101(a)(42)(A) and (B) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) and (B), which includes the requirement that they are not a persecutor. When USCIS discovers after an alien’s admission to the United States that they should not have been admitted because they did not meet the refugee definition and therefore the eligibility requirements for refugee classification at the time of admission, it is important to protect the integrity of the American immigration system by taking whatever steps are legally available, including ensuring that the alien is removed from the United States as quickly as possible where there is a legal basis to do so. There is an inherent risk to national security and public safety when an alien’s identity has not been fully established. Therefore, the ability to streamline refugee status termination, where appropriate, contributes immediately to the safety of the American people and the integrity of the lawful U.S. immigration system.

The current notice and response process for terminating refugee status upon determination that the alien was not a refugee at the time of their admission is inefficient and compromises the security and safety of the United States. Providing 30 days to respond to a NOIT, instead of a 10-day response period, allows ineligible aliens more time to retain immigration benefits to which they are not entitled, undermining the integrity of the U.S. immigration system and national interests of the United States. Moreover, when an alien retains a status he or she is not entitled to, while also being inadequately vetted with insufficient information as to their true identity, there is a risk to American society’s safety and security.

B. Legal Authority The Secretary of Homeland Security’s (Secretary) authority for the regulatory amendment made in this IFR is found in various provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA), Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135 (codified in part at 6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). Under the INA, the Secretary has authority over the admission, termination of status, removal, and adjustment of status of refugees. See, e.g., INA 207, 209, 8 U.S.C. 1157, 1159.4 Most importantly, section 207(c)(4) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4), allows the Secretary to terminate the refugee status of any alien and the alien’s spouse or children if the Secretary determines that the alien “was not in fact a refugee . . . at the time of the alien’s admission” and expressly authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations governing the 4 See also HSA 451(b)(3), (5), 6 U.S.C. 271(b)(3), (5) (transferring the authority to adjudicate refugee applications and other adjudications performed before the enactment of the HSA from the Immigration and Naturalization Service (“INS”) to DHS).

procedures for such terminations. The Secretary has delegated the authority to grant refugee status and to adjust or terminate such status to USCIS.5 General authority for issuing this IFR is found in section 103(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a), which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 112, which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations.6 Additional authority for this rule is found in:

•Section 101(b)(1)(F) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F), which establishes as a primary mission of DHS the duty to, “ensure that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland;” •Section 101(a)(42) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), which defines a refugee; and •Section 451(a)(3) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 271(a)(3), which confers authority on the USCIS Director to establish “policies for performing [immigration adjudication] functions.” C. Summary of the Regulatory Action Through this IFR, DHS is amending 8 CFR 207.9 to change the 30-day notice- and-response period for aliens whose refugee status is terminated by USCIS to a 10-day notice-and-response period.

5 See DHS, Delegation to the Bureau of Citizenship and Immigration Services, No. 0150.1 (June 5, 2003), https://www.hsdl.org/?abstract&did=234775; see also 8 CFR 207.4, 207.9; 8 CFR 209.1. 6 Although several provisions of the INA discussed in this IFR refer exclusively to the “Attorney General,” such provisions are now to be read as referring to the Secretary by operation of the HSA. See 6 U.S.C. 202(3), 251, 271(b), 542 note, and 557; 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1) and (g), 1551 note; Nielsen v. Preap, 586 U.S. 392, 397 n.2 (2019).

D. Related Rulemakings DHS is engaging in multiple rulemaking actions that are in various stages of development.7 DHS has considered and analyzed each of these rules for peripheral, overlapping, and interrelated effects on this rule and has found none, as this IFR is narrowly focused on refugee termination procedures.

DHS has also, to the extent possible, considered the effects, if any, of possible policy changes of which USCIS is aware. For example, a memorandum issued jointly by ICE and USCIS on February 18, 2026, impacting individuals with refugee status states, “the policy of USCIS and ICE regarding when, and under what circumstances, immigration officers may detain refugees who have failed to adjust to lawful permanent resident status.”8 The policy changes announced in the memo relate to the statutory requirement at INA 209, 8 U.S.C. 1159, governing the conditional admission of refugees and their adjustment of status, and provide that DHS may arrest and detain a refugee who has lived in the United States for at least one year and has not yet acquired LPR status under INA 209(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1159(a)(1), to inspect and examine the refugee for admission as an LPR.9 While the policy changes are similarly aimed at protecting the public interest through vetting of aliens admitted as refugees, including vetting for national security, public safety, and fraud-related issues, the focus of this rule is on procedures in terminations cases, not the custody, arrest or detention of a refugee who has failed to adjust status.

7 See Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, “2026 Regulatory Plan and the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions,” https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaMain (last visited July 15, 2026).

8 Memorandum from Joseph B. Edlow, Director, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, and Todd M. Lyons, Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, “Detention of Refugees Who Have Failed to Adjust to Lawful Permanent Resident Status,” (Feb. 18, 2026). 9 On March 23, 2026, a U.S. District Court in the District of Massachusetts stayed DHS’s adoption and implementation of the policies outlined in the February 18, 2026, Memo related to the arrest and detention of refugees who have lived in the United States for more than one year and have not acquired LPR status. See Jean A. v. Noem, 2026 WL 805207, at * 1 (D. Mass. Mar. 23, 2026).
DHS invites the public to submit comments during the 30-day comment period regarding anticipated interaction with related rules and policy changes.

III. Background and Purpose A. Initial Refugee Processing Refugee status in the United States is a highly sought after immigration benefit for displaced persons throughout the world due in part to the benefits it bestows as well as a pathway to permanent status. Resettlement to the United States through the United States Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) is a multi-step process involving several agency partners. The U.S. Department of State (State) leads the annual consultations process, funds and oversees refugee resettlement activities, contracts with the non- governmental organizations that provide pre- and post-USCIS interview support, and facilitates the Priority 1 referrals to the USRAP process. After an alien is determined to have access to the USRAP, they may file a Form I-590, Registration for Classification as Refugee.10 Applications for refugee classification are primarily processed overseas and adjudicated by USCIS Refugee Officers who determine whether an alien meets the refugee definition and is otherwise eligible for resettlement to the United States. Under United States law, to be eligible for refugee classification an applicant must establish that he or she:
•is located outside the country of his or her nationality; 11 •is of special humanitarian concern to the United States;
•was persecuted or fears persecution due to race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social group;

USCIS officers make a determination of eligibility for refugee classification based on the above elements of eligibility. USCIS approval of an application for refugee classification authorizes U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to admit the alien “conditionally” as a refugee upon arrival at a U.S. port of entry within four months of the date of such approval.12 U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of Refugee Resettlement provides resettlement assistance, that includes employment training, English language training, cash assistance (in a manner that promotes early self- sufficiency), and job placement, to the aliens admitted as refugees to the United States. Derivatives of the principal refugee applicant may include the spouse of a principal refugee and their unmarried children under the age of 21.13 Derivative family members may be included in the initial application for refugee status or petitioned for after the principal refugee’s arrival to the United States. Id. For derivatives to be admitted to the United States as refugees, they must establish that they are admissible and not subject to the persecutor bar but are not required to prove that they meet the refugee definition or any of its elements, such as past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution.

B. Termination of Refugee Status The sole basis for USCIS to terminate the status of an alien conditionally admitted to the United States as a refugee is if USCIS determines that the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of admission to the United States.15 No other ground of termination is specified under the law. An alien who did not, in fact, meet the refugee definition at the time of admission would have been inadmissible, and once that status is terminated, will generally lack legal grounds to remain in the United States.16 The determination to terminate refugee status because the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of his or her admission to the United States applies solely to principal refugees and not to derivative refugees. In order to be eligible for refugee status, principal applicants must meet the requirements of the refugee definition in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), must be admissible to the United States, and must qualify under one of the designated USRAP processing priorities.17 USCIS may in turn terminate a derivative refugee’s status if the principal’s status is terminated.18 Refugee status can only be terminated while the alien remains in refugee status and has not yet adjusted to lawful permanent resident (LPR) status or naturalized.19 However, if USCIS has rescinded an alien’s LPR status under INA 246, 8 U.S.C. 1156, an alien admitted as a refugee reverts to the prior refugee status and his or her refugee status can be terminated if the basis for termination meets the statutory requirements.20 15 INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4).

The NOIT further informs the alien of his or her right to offer written or oral evidence in support of his or her refugee claim and in opposition to the proposed termination. More truncated, less thorough interviews under the Biden administration damaged the integrity of refugee processing by hindering the officers’ ability to appropriately gather sufficient information 32 Revised Guidance on Informal (“Camp”) Marriage, Memo, RAIO Acting Associate Director T. Kim (Feb. 14, 2022)].

33 8 CFR 207.2 (requiring that “[e]ach applicant 14 years old or older shall appear in person before an immigration officer for inquiry under oath to determine their eligibility for admission as a refugee”). 34 USCIS RAIO Lesson Plan, Interviewing-Introduction to the Non-Adversarial Interview (Dec. 13, 2024). related to the aforementioned purposes of the refugee interview and to make an appropriate and legally sufficient decision. Consequently, these changes enabled ineligible aliens to exploit the refugee program to resettle in the United States, where they then have a path to permanent status, including citizenship.

USCIS further instructed its adjudicators that it was no longer necessary to ask additional detailed questions to identify and explore inadmissibility grounds, including security-related inadmissibility grounds, absent a clear indication of a concern. For example, per internal guidance, if an alien was transported across a border by smugglers, or an alien’s home was attacked by an armed group, absent additional information in the record or in country conditions information indicating possible security-related concerns with respect to these incidents (e.g., material support to a terrorist organization), officers were not required to follow up or explore if the individual was potentially inadmissible, or if these interactions raised other concerns. Officers were discouraged from investigating potential concerns or delving into an applicant’s background or past experiences unless referral documents, such as the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Resettlement Registration Form (RRF), explicitly noted concerns. In other words, officers were discouraged from seeking or obtaining additional information beyond what was provided in the record, already provided by non-U.S. government entities, such as UNHCR or the Resettlement Support Center.

With respect to country of origin information (COI), rather than using COI to inform their interviews and adjudications, USCIS, under the Biden administration, trained refugee officers that for certain populations, they could rely on COI “profiles” (e.g. “Venezuelans who oppose the government of Venezuela”) to establish various elements of refugee eligibility once an alien indicated they were part of a group of individuals for which COI supported a finding of well-founded fear. Officers shifted from individualized, more detailed assessments of refugee eligibility to confining interviews to review of the Form I-590 and an alien’s affirmation of belonging to a designated group (e.g., Rohingya), rather than exploring and evaluating an alien’s unique experiences of past persecution or fears. In doing so, they bypassed in-depth interviews exploring an alien’s background, experiences of past persecution in their home country, affiliations and relationships, if the alien in fact had a well-founded fear of future persecution in their home country, and other relevant details.

In 2017, President Trump issued Executive Order 13769, Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States, restricting entry to the U.S. by certain foreign nationals and temporarily suspending the USRAP.35 During this suspension of refugee processing agencies were directed to review and strengthen vetting procedures. As a result of the review, USCIS clarified and confirmed that as a matter of policy, officers interviewing refugee applicants were required to elicit sufficient information to make a determination on both the past persecution and well-founded fear of future persecution claims. Gathering testimony on both past persecution and well- founded fear ensures a thorough and accurate evaluation of the applicant’s eligibility and prevents overlooking critical facts that could substantiate, or call into question, their claim. For example, thorough elicitation of testimony regarding past and future harm may help identify inconsistencies and potential fraud by allowing adjudicators to probe the alien’s narrative for credibility by ensuring it is internally consistent and consistent with statements the alien may have provided to processing partners prior to interview. Most importantly, it requires officers to probe more thoroughly into an applicant’s background and experiences, helping to establish his or her identity, and further ensure that the correct decision is made in his or her case. Although eliciting testimony about both past persecution and well-founded fear helps develop a fuller picture of the alien and better assess eligibility—ensuring that protection is granted to those who genuinely 35 Protecting the Nation From Foreign Terrorist Entry Into the United States, 82 FR 8977 (Feb. 1, 2017). qualify under the law—during the Biden administration this policy was rescinded. Refugee officers were no longer required to elicit testimony on both past persecution and well-founded fear claims, and were instead instructed to only pursue one or the other, once one had been established, precluding opportunities to identify critical information and concerns related to an alien’s eligibility.

In addition to the relaxed requirements for principal refugee applicants, USCIS changed policies regarding derivative applicants. The first Trump administration issued guidance emphasizing the importance of eliciting testimony from derivative I-590 applicants apart from the principal refugee applicant to further explore potential national security, identity, inadmissibility, and credibility issues. However, USCIS subsequently rescinded this guidance under the Biden administration and provided refugee officers the sole discretion on when to interview derivative applicants separately. The purpose of this change was to reduce the amount of questions and time spent with derivatives in an interview, thus not thoroughly vetting and identifying potential issues of all members of a case who, upon case approval, were eligible to travel to the United States as refugees along with the principal applicant.

Compounding the issue, marriage guidance under the previous administration relaxed the criteria for adding a derivative spouse to a case. Although intended to accommodate couples who genuinely acted as spouses but could not formalize their union due to local restrictions, the standards were misapplied, allowing individuals with minimal or short-term connections to be classified as spouses and included on cases. This practice, combined with lowered interview standards and increasingly brief, less detailed case reviews in the name of streamlining, increased the risk of approving applicants with only tenuous relationships with the principal applicant.

In parallel with this minimized focus on eliciting substantive information to comprehensively understand an alien’s background and identify potential issues of concern, the increased interview quotas made it more difficult for officers to explore important issues, fully probe the alien’s credibility, and still meet their productivity expectations. During the first Trump administration, USCIS reduced the number of refugee interviews conducted per day per officer for certain cases to allow for further exploration of potential national security, inadmissibility, and credibility issues at interviews for refugee adjudications. Notwithstanding, USCIS under the Biden administration, in their effort to streamline interviews and increase the volume of refugee cases that could be processed, increased the number of cases an officer was expected to interview and adjudicate in a day for certain cases, again pressuring officers to at times scale back interviews to comply with the expectations.

This shift away from in-depth, thorough interviews in order to streamline and expedite admission of aliens to the United States as refugees shut down important lines of questioning to identify potential national security, public safety, and other concerns to accurately assess eligibility, illustrating the program’s emphasis on the volume of refugee case completions rather than the quality of interviews or the integrity of adjudications. Refugee officers potentially missed vital information that could impact an applicant’s eligibility, including issues related to fraud, public safety, and national security, and discretionary factors. USCIS, under the Biden administration, failed to fulfill its responsibility to ensure that its officers thoroughly assessed applicants, potentially resulting in an influx of ineligible aliens into the country that may pose a risk to the national interests of the United States.

Moreover, USCIS under the Biden administration decreased requirements for supervisory review of refugee cases by only requiring review of the assessment in lieu of reviewing the entire case contents. This limited supervisor oversight to ensure cases were thoroughly and accurately adjudicated, increased the risk that important information about an alien was overlooked.

An overarching desire to approve as many refugee cases as possible to meet the refugee ceiling set by the Biden administration contributed to a culture in which the expectation appeared to be to approve cases, even where egregious concerns may have existed. For instance, in one processing location, a number of aliens identified as having defrauded the U.S. government or submitting fraudulent documentation were found inadmissible pursuant to the INA provisions related to fraud and misrepresentation. Despite clear evidence of misrepresentation, including falsification of identity and key information relevant to their access to the USRAP, USCIS almost universally approved waivers of the misrepresentation or fraud. This pattern demonstrates a troubling disregard for the integrity of the refugee program, as individuals who had already demonstrated a willingness to engage in fraud and misrepresentation of their identities to U.S. government officials, were nonetheless permitted to proceed with resettlement to the United States, undermining both the security and credibility of the admissions process. The persistent presence of individuals, both in the United States and overseas, attempting to exploit and defraud the U.S. humanitarian programs, poses risks to national security, public safety, and the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. Historically, DHS and State have identified, through investigations, fraud concerns among the special humanitarian access categories. For example, in January 2021, DHS and State suspended the Iraqi Direct Access P-2 Program, following an extensive investigation carried out by the State Diplomatic Security Service and the DHS Office of the Inspector General, which uncovered a fraud scheme related to the program.36 According to the indictment and statement of facts agreed to by one of the three defendants in the criminal case against the individuals:

from approximately February 2016 until at least April 2019, the three defendants, led by Abduljabbar, conspired to steal U.S. government records 36 See DHS Office of Inspector General, “Iraqi National Pleads Guilty to Conspiracy To Defraud U.S. Refugee Program,” (Jan. 26, 2022), https://www.oig.dhs.gov/news/press-releases/2022/01262022/iraqi- national-pleads-guilty-conspiracy-defraud-us-refugee-program.

IV. Discussion of Interim Final Rule Previous administrations’ prioritization of the admissions of large numbers of refugees over homeland security blatantly overlooked essential components of eligibility and put at risk the national security, public safety and other interests of the U.S. citizenry. Safeguarding national security and public safety remains the foremost priority of the country’s immigration programs, taking precedence over numerical admission targets. The agency stands committed to conducting rigorous vetting of all aliens and to the detection and prevention of fraud and other serious threats, ensuring the safety of all Americans prior to admission of an alien to the United States.

Accordingly, this IFR shortens the amount of time that refugees are provided to respond to a NOIT in order to ensure that terminations of refugee status can occur as expeditiously as possible to protect national security and public safety, given the risks created by the deficient vetting described above in Section III.C. Under this IFR, refugees will continue to receive a NOIT, which will specify DHS’s intent to terminate their refugee status based on a determination that they did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission. DHS will provide the specific reason or reasons why USCIS found the refugee failed to meet the refugee definition at the time of admission (e.g., failure to establish that past harm experienced was serious enough to rise to the level of persecution, a determination that the alien’s harm was not on account of a protected ground, failure to provide credible testimony as to any or all of the elements of the refugee definition, etc.). However, this rule will provide such aliens with ten days (rather than 30 days) to respond (provide documentary evidence or indicate a desire to provide oral evidence) if they choose. If the deadline to reply to the NOIT passes without a response, the refugee is considered to have forfeited his or her right to rebut the allegations in the NOIT, and DHS will terminate his or her refugee status.

By regulation, the response period begins either upon personal service of the NOIT directly to the alien or, if sent by mail, upon mailing of the NOIT.52 When calculating the response deadline, all days, including Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, are counted.53 However, if the final day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday, the deadline is extended to the next business day.54 Per 8 CFR 103.8(b), if the notice is served by mail, three days are added to the response period, with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed.

DHS’s foremost priority is the safety and security of American citizens and residents. At the same time, DHS is committed to ensuring that refugees who receive a NOIT are afforded a meaningful opportunity to respond or provide a rebuttal. To enhance mail service reliability and afford refugees the full response period, DHS will utilize express delivery service providers, which guarantee a three-day delivery window and offer tracking and confirmation of both the NOIT’s departure from DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient.55 This approach ensures that refugees receive their NOIT promptly and can exercise their right to respond. The NOIT will be dated on the day it is mailed, and the 10-day response period for the refugee will begin from that date. If the 52 8 CFR 103.8.

54 Id.

55 See, e.g., https://www.fedex.com/en-us/shipping/3-day-express-saver-shipping.html. refugee wishes to request an opportunity to provide oral testimony in lieu of responding to each point or points in the NOIT, such a request would be considered a timely response by DHS. As explained above, in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8(b), when a notice is served by mail, three additional days are added to the response period, with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed. Therefore, applicants who are mailed notices are afforded a total of 13 days to respond, accounting for this regulatory provision.

Reducing the 30-day response timeframe for NOITs issued in refugee terminations to a 10-day response timeframe allows DHS to take swifter action in cases where aliens did not meet the definition of a refugee when admitted to the United States. USCIS needs the ability to terminate refugee status in such cases in order to more quickly begin the removal process for aliens who should never have been admitted to the United States as refugees in the first place, including aliens similarly situated to those discussed above in Section III.C, who also pose a national security or public safety risk. While termination of refugee status is not a precondition for initiation of removal proceedings, the termination of refugee status gives DHS a statutory basis for removal, and in some cases, no other removal grounds apply, so this termination is needed.56 Accordingly, promptly terminating refugee status in cases where the alien was clearly ineligible at the time of admission facilitates DHS’s ability to process the alien for removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA, and to remove the alien if they do not qualify for relief from removal.

56 In Matter of Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836 (BIA 2005), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that termination of an alien’s refugee status under section 207 of the INA is not a precondition to the initiation of section 240 removal proceedings, but only because the alien in that case was removable on the basis of certain criminal conduct that independently qualified him for removal irrespective of refugee status. See id. at 837-838; compare Matter of D-K-, 25 I&N Dec. 761 (BIA 2012) (affirming that DHS need not terminate refugee status prior to commencing section 240 removal proceedings but determining that the alien was not removable under the grounds charged by DHS). On January 21, 2026, the DHS Secretary formally referred the BIA’s decision in Matter of D-K- to the Attorney General for review. In that referral, DHS asked the Attorney General to vacate the BIA’s decision insofar as it erroneously holds that aliens admitted as refugees may not be taken back into DHS custody under section 209(a)(l) of the INA, charged with inadmissibility under section 212(a) of the INA, and promptly removed.

More broadly, timely termination of their refugee status is critical to the integrity of the country’s immigration programs, considering the risks they may pose to the United States. As USCIS continues to encounter aliens admitted as refugees who did not meet the definition of refugee at the time of admission, termination of refugee status in as prompt and efficient manner as possible ensures USCIS can best protect the safety and security of Americans and continue complying with E.O.s 14161 and 14163. By shortening the 30-day period for an alien to respond to a NOIT to 10 days, USCIS is exercising its authority to expeditiously terminate the status of refugees who did not meet the refugee definition at the time of their admission to the United States. Streamlining the termination process additionally ensures that ineligible aliens who were erroneously allowed to enter the United States as refugees lose their authorization to work in as timely a manner as possible since termination of refugee status also results in termination of employment authorization.

DHS believes that reducing the NOIT response period from 30 days to 10 days maintains adequate procedural safeguards for aliens by affording them an opportunity to respond to the NOIT while also balancing the government’s interests in national security and public safety and in protecting the integrity of the refugee program. The NOIT will inform the alien the basis for termination and explain that they may submit evidence to contest termination, and/or request an interview. An alien does not need to submit evidence or a full response within the 10 days, and may instead opt for an interview, but must make the interview request to USCIS within the response period. Aliens who receive a NOIT under the proposed process therefore will continue to receive a meaningful opportunity to respond to the allegations in the notice—the alien can submit a written response to the NOIT within the deadline and/or request an interview with USCIS where their refugee claim can be heard. The abbreviated time period to respond to the NOIT will in turn allow the government to more efficiently process cases where aliens did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission to the United States, and who were from the outset, never eligible for the benefit they received. Instead of waiting 30 days for an alien to respond to a NOIT before scheduling an interview if requested by the alien or taking other action, this rule will allow USCIS to act as soon as 10 days after service of the NOIT. For aliens who do not respond timely, the 10-day response period will allow USCIS to finalize termination much more quickly. Furthermore, each alien whose refugee status is terminated will be processed under INA sections 235, 240, or 241 and may seek other forms of relief or protection from removal as permitted in those proceedings. For example, aliens in section 240 removal proceedings may seek other forms of relief in a hearing before an immigration judge where the interests of the U.S. Government are properly represented by an attorney from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA).

The regulatory amendment being made in this IFR is clearly authorized by INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4), which gives discretion to the Secretary to “prescribe” regulations governing termination of aliens who were “not in fact a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) . . . at the time of the alien’s admission.” V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements A. Administrative Procedures Act (APA) DHS is issuing this IFR without prior notice or public procedure because DHS is invoking the “good cause” and foreign affairs exceptions of the APA. See 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1), (b)(B). For the same reasons, a delayed effective date of no less than 30 days is not required under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3). DHS has also considered potential reliance interests and discusses them below.

a. Good Cause An agency may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed effective date when the agency “for good cause finds . . . that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). Likewise, section 553(d)'s requirement of 30-day advance publication may be waived by the agency for good cause found and published with the rule. See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3).

The “impracticable” prong of the good cause exception excuses notice and comment in emergency situations, or where the delay caused by the APA's notice-and- comment procedures would result in serious harm to life, property, or an immediate threat to public safety.57 Although the good cause exception is “narrowly construed and only reluctantly countenanced,”58 it is an important safety valve to be used where delay caused by notice and comment would do real harm (even absent an emergency situation).59 An agency may find that advance notice and comment or a delayed effective date is “impracticable” when undertaking such procedure would impede due and timely execution of an important agency function.60 For example, courts have explained that notice-and-comment rulemaking may be impracticable where, for instance, air travel security would be unable to address threats posing a “possible imminent hazard to aircraft, persons and property within the United States;”61 if a rule was of life-saving importance to mine workers in the event of a mine explosion;62 if public safety is 57 See Nat. DHS is immediately taking measures to implement a process that changes the 30-day response timeframe in refugee termination cases to 10 days, thereby expediting terminations in a manner that averts harm to the public.

Engaging in the APA’s notice-and-comment requirement under 5 U.S.C. 553(b) would impede DHS’s duties as outlined in E.O. 14161, requiring that sufficient safeguards are in place to prevent any refugee from being admitted to the United States without undergoing stringent vetting, and E.O. 14163, permitting admission of refugees on a case-by-case basis only so long as it is determined to be in the national interest and the alien does not pose a threat to the security and welfare of the United States. Thus, in accordance with President Trump's policy determinations related to foreign nationals, DHS is taking, without delay, immediate action to ensure that aliens who did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission to the United States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible to ensure they do not receive significant benefits, including employment authorization, permanent legal status, and other federal, state, and local benefits. Furthermore, unless DHS acts immediately, there is a risk that aliens who were not eligible for admission as refugees could present harm to the public interest.

As explained in detail in Section IV of this preamble, DHS reasonably believes, based on a review of prior refugee approvals and internal procedures, policies, and directives, that the lack of detailed refugee interviews and insufficient inquiry into critical matters such as inadmissibilities or terrorism-related grounds, coupled with the prioritization of admission numbers over legally sufficient decisions and other programmatic issues like over-reliance on COI, have resulted in aliens receiving refugee status when they were not eligible. These practices have compromised the integrity of the refugee program.

In Operation PARRIS, DHS has further identified similar issues regarding the quality of refugee interviews after reviewing a subset of cases, where in some instances populations from specific countries were processed and approved with minimal lines of questioning. This rule amends the 30-day period to 10 days for aliens to respond to a NOIT so that the agency can expeditiously issue terminations in cases where, after a thorough review of the case and comprehensive vetting, USCIS determines that the alien did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission. In such cases, an alien will not maintain valid refugee status a day longer than legally required. This IFR would accordingly more quickly eliminate a pathway to permanent status used by aliens with falsified claims or malevolent intent, including those who may pose an ongoing and imminent threat to public safety and national security such as the refugee cases reviewed and terminated by the USCIS Vetting Center outlined above.

Therefore, if DHS had to engage in advance notice-and-comment procedures, it would continue to allow aliens who should have never been admitted to the United States as refugees to remain present longer than necessary, potentially putting at risk the safety and security of the United States and compromising the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. For example, in one case, after admission to the U.S. it was later discovered that the refugee was a war criminal who should have been subject to the persecutor bar and not allowed into the country. In another case listed above, the refugee was not admissible due to a lack of credibility with regard to both participation in and sending money to the OLF (a Tier III terrorist organization at the time of the alien’s involvement) as well as his father’s status as a well-known OLF member. In these circumstances, providing advance notice-and-comment procedures is impracticable and not in the public interest. Finally, DHS finds that it is unnecessary to delay this final rule’s effective date under 5 U.S.C. 553(d). There is no need to give affected parties additional time to adjust their behavior before this final rule takes effect because DHS believes there are likely no behavioral adjustments to make. The aliens who would be affected by this rule have already entered the United States.69 In other words, a delay in the rule’s effective date would be unlikely to have an impact on an alien’s choice to seek to enter the United States as a refugee or not and would not impact whether or not they were eligible for such status at the time of admission. A delayed effective date would serve no purpose but create further harm to the public, as exemplified by the cases that, upon review and additional vetting, have resulted in the issuance of NOITs because the record indicated the alien was not a refugee at the time of admission.

For the reasons outlined above, DHS believes that bypassing the ordinary notice- and-comment procedures and the delayed effective date requirement is justified, under the totality of circumstances, and given that immediate action is necessary, is consistent with DHS’s statutory mission to take regulatory action to administer the refugee program effectively, as well as the President’s directives in E.O. 14161 and E.O. 14163. Nevertheless, recognizing the value of public comments, DHS is publishing this rule as an IFR with a request for public comment.

The replacement costs typically include expenses of advertising positions, search and agency fees, screening applicants, interviews, background verification, employment testing, hiring bonuses, and possible travel and relocation costs. Once hired, employers face additional training, orientation, and assessment costs.

Second, there can be costs for productivity and possibly profitability due to operational and production disruptions, which can include errors from other employees that may temporally fill the position. A third cost segment, which is a type of indirect 80 For a description of these costs, see “Employee Retention: The Real Cost of Losing an Employee,” by Holly Bengfort, PeopleKeep (updated Dec. 15, 2025), at: https://www.peoplekeep.com/blog/Employee- Retention-The-Real-Cost-of-Losing-an-Employee. See also, “This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion,” by Shane McFeely and Ben Wigert, Gallup Workplace (Mar. 13, 2019) at: https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx. cost, can encompass loss of institutional knowledge, networking, and impacts to work culture, morale, and interpersonal relationships.

DHS is providing a 10-day, as opposed to the current 30-day, timeframe to contest applicable NOITs. The NOIT will inform the alien the basis for termination and explain that they may submit evidence to contest termination, and/or request an interview. Aliens who would currently respond to a NOIT to attempt to reaffirm their status would sustain some direct costs and also opportunity costs of time applicable to generating and preparing responses, organizing documents and evidence, and participating in interviews. Under the 10-day timeframe, such resourcing and expenditure would likely still be incurred, but the timeframe would be contracted. There could be impacts and costs to aliens applicable to having less time to collect evidence, prepare documentation, and prepare their response.

As is pertinent to the public sector, planned extensive vetting, case review, and reinterviews, as well as enforcement operations for the Federal Bureau of Investigation and ICE, in support directly or indirectly of this IFR, could require an increase in public resources. As is applicable to mailing the NOITs, DHS will utilize express delivery service providers, which guarantee delivery within the IFR timeframe, and offers tracking and confirmation of both the package’s departure from DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient. This is not a significant change from current practice and DHS does not expect that this IFR will generate additional costs applicable to mailing the NOITs. USCIS will continue to expend resources on processing and review of the responses. However, the revised timeline may generate efficiencies as USCIS will be able to schedule interviews or take action more quickly. DHS cannot predict in advance the net effect to public resources and welcomes public input concerning public sector resources. DHS, however, does not and cannot assert that it knows and has considered every policy change that may occur at all levels and agencies of the U.S. government that may directly or indirectly affect this IFR. Therefore, there could be other impacts not currently described in this discussion.

DHS cannot quantify the benefits of this IFR but believes that increased national security, public safety, credibility, and reduced fraud or misrepresentation by applicable aliens, among other concerns, will contribute to the safety of the American people and integrity of the lawful United States immigration system to the extent that the benefits will outweigh any costs. Streamlining the process to terminate refugee status in cases where the alien is determined to not have been a refugee at the time of admission to the United States is consistent with the DHS mission and responsibilities to ensure national security and public safety and beneficially protects the immigration system from fraud and exploitation.

The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. The RFA's regulatory flexibility analysis requirements apply only to those rules for which an agency is required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553 or any other law.81 DHS did not issue a notice of proposed rulemaking for this action.

J. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) DHS and its components analyze final actions to determine whether the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq., applies and, if so, what degree of analysis is required. DHS Directive 023-01, Rev. 01“Implementing the National Environmental Policy Act” (Directive 023-01) and Instruction Manual 023-01- 001-01 Revision 01, “Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act” (Instruction Manual)84 established the policies and procedures that DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.

NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA implementing procedures, categories of actions (“categorical exclusions”) that experience has shown do not, individually or cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.85 The Instruction Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS Categorical Exclusions.86 Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more of the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the potential for a significant environmental effect.87 This IFR is strictly administrative and procedural because it is only amending an existing DHS regulation governing the termination of refugee status. DHS has reviewed this IFR and finds that no significant impact on the environment, or any change in environmental effect will result from the amendments being promulgated in this rule. Accordingly, DHS finds that the promulgation of this IFR’s amendments to a current regulation clearly fits within the categorical exclusion A3 established in DHS’s NEPA implementing procedures as an administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not part of a larger Federal action, and does not present extraordinary circumstances that create the potential for a significant environmental effect. Therefore, these regulatory amendments are categorically excluded from further NEPA review.

Accordingly, for the reasons set forth in the preamble, DHS amends 8 CFR part 207 as follows:
PART 207-ADMISSION OF REFUGEES
1. The authority citation for part 207 continues to read as follows:
2. Revise § 207.9 to read as follows:
§ 207.9 Termination of refugee status.

The refugee status of any alien (and of the spouse or child of the alien) admitted to the United States under section 207 of the Act will be terminated by USCIS if the alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Act at the time of admission. USCIS will notify the alien in writing of its intent to terminate the alien's refugee status. The alien will have 10 days from the date notice is served upon him or her in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8 to present written or oral evidence to show why the alien’s refugee status should not be terminated. There is no appeal under this chapter from the termination of refugee status by USCIS. Upon termination of refugee status, USCIS will process the alien under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the Act.

DHS는 또한 본 IFR로 인해 발생할 수 있는 경제적, 환경적 또는 연방주의적 영향과 관련된 의견도 요청합니다. 의견은 영어로 제출되어야 하며, 그렇지 않을 경우 영어 번역본을 함께 제출하여야 합니다. 미국 시민권이민서비스국(USCIS)이 이러한 변경사항을 시행하는 데 가장 큰 도움이 되는 의견은 IFR의 특정 부분을 인용하고, 권고하는 변경에 대한 이유를 설명하며, 그러한 권고 변경을 뒷받침하는 자료, 정보 또는 근거를 포함하는 의견입니다. 위에 열거된 방법 이외의 방식으로 제출된 의견, 즉 DHS 또는 USCIS 관계자에게 발송된 이메일이나 서신 등은 본 IFR에 대한 의견으로 간주되지 아니하며, DHS로부터 답변을 받지 못할 수 있습니다.

안내사항: 의견을 제출하는 경우, 귀하는 기관명(U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, 미국 시민권이민서비스국)과 본 규칙제정에 대한 DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397을 반드시 포함하여야 합니다. 의견 또는 자료 제출에 사용된 방법과 관계없이, 모든 제출물은 변경 없이 연방 전자규칙제정포털(Federal eRulemaking Portal)인 https://www.regulations.gov 에 게시되며, 여기에는 귀하가 제공하는 모든 개인정보가 포함됩니다. 따라서 이러한 정보를 제출하는 것은 그 정보를 공개하는 것이 됩니다. 귀하는 DHS에 제출하는 자발적인 공개 의견서에 포함시키는 개인정보의 양을 제한하는 것을 고려할 수 있습니다. DHS는 개인의 사생활에 영향을 미칠 수 있거나 불쾌감을 줄 수 있다고 판단하는 의견서 내의 정보를 공개 열람으로부터 보류할 수 있습니다. 추가 정보는 https://www.regulations.gov 에서 확인할 수 있는 개인정보 보호 및 보안 고지(Privacy and Security Notice)를 참조하시기 바랍니다.
접수기록부: 접수기록부에 접속하거나 배경 문서 또는 접수된 의견을 열람하려면, DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0397을 참조하여 https://www.regulations.gov 로 이동하십시오. 의견이 게시되거나 최종규칙이 공표될 때 알림을 받기 위하여 온라인 접수기록부에서 이메일 알림을 신청할 수도 있습니다.

II. 개요
A. 규제 조치의 목적
이 규칙 제정의 목적은 실제로는 입국 당시 난민 분류 자격이 없었음에도 난민으로 미국에 입국이 허가된 외국인으로 인해 발생할 수 있는 잠재적 위험을 완화하기 위하여 종료 통지 기간을 단축하는 것입니다. 부적절하게 입국이 허가된 자는 불완전한 기록으로 인해 신원이 완전히 확인되고 심사되지 않았을 수 있으며, 이에 따라 프로그램의 무결성에 위험을 초래하고 국가안보 및 공공안전에 위험을 초래할 수 있습니다. 바이든 행정부 하에서 시행된 난민 처리 정책 및 절차에 대한 검토 결과, 외국인의 신원, 난민 분류 자격, 입국 가능성이 불완전한 기록에 근거하여 결정된 채 난민으로 미국에 입국이 허가되는 등 무결성이 심각하게 훼손되었음을 알 수 있습니다.1 이 기간 동안 시행된 운영 지침은 심사관이 통상적인 질의 절차를 생략할 수 있도록 허용하였으며, 이로 인해 난민 심사 절차의 핵심적인 심사 요소인 난민 면접의 수준과 실효성이 희생되었습니다.2 품질보다 신속성을 우선시함으로써 철저하지 못한 면접이 조장되었습니다. 외국인이 미국에 입국하기 전에 난민 지위 자격을 갖추었는지 확인하기 위한 특정 질문들이 1 난민 신청자는 이민 혜택을 위한 목적으로 자신의 신원을 입증할 책임이 있습니다. 신원은 신청자가 본인이 주장하는 사람임을 확인하는 데 도움이 되므로 난민 심사에서 핵심적인 요소입니다. 신원은 생체 정보, 서류 증거 및 진술의 수집을 통해 입증될 수 있습니다. 난민의 맥락에서 진술은 주요한 증거 자료입니다. 이는 신청자의 배경, 가족 관계, 과거 경험 및 교우 관계에 관한 유용한 정보를 제공하며, 이는 신청자가 어떠한 사람인지, 그리고 신청하는 혜택에 대한 자격이 있는지를 확인하는 데 맥락을 제공합니다. 신청자가 미국 정부가 만족할 수 있도록 자신의 신원을 입증하여 당국이 신청자의 신원에 대하여 확신을 가질 수 있도록 하는 능력은 신청된 이민 혜택에 대한 자격 결정에 필요한 단계입니다.
2 미네소타주에 거주하는 재정착 난민 사례들은 ICE 및 FBI를 포함한 다른 법집행 기관 파트너들과 함께 수행된 Operation Twin Shield와 같은 최근의 공동 사기 방지 집행 조치를 강화하기 위한 초기 시범 운영 집단의 일환으로 검토되었습니다.

생략되었으며, 이로 인해 자격이 없는 외국인이 난민 분류 승인을 받고 이어서 미국에 입국하게 될 위험이 증가하였습니다. 이는 바이든 행정부 재임 기간 중 면접, 승인 및 입국이 이루어진 미네소타주 거주 입국 난민에 대한 최근의 예비 검토를 통하여 뒷받침됩니다. 검토된 사건들의 대다수에서, 주 신청자가 난민 정의의 모든 필수 요건을 충족하였음을 입증할 증거가 불충분하였습니다.3 그 목표는 바이든 대통령의 난민 입국 상한을 충족하기 위하여 실행 가능한 한 많은 난민을 미국에 입국시키는 것이었으며, 이를 달성하기 위하여 철저한 심사 및 자격 평가를 보장하기 위한 다수의 요건이 축소되거나 제거되었습니다.

이는 난민 프로그램의 무결성에 대한 우려를 제기하며, 이 기간 동안 미국에 입국이 허가된 외국인의 난민 지위 자격에 의문을 제기합니다. 이 전문에서 아래에 상세히 설명하는 바와 같이, 난민 프로그램 내의 무결성 조치를 현저히 축소시키는 여러 정책 결정이 시행되었습니다. 이러한 변화로 인하여 심사관 1인당 하루에 수행하는 난민 면접 건수가 증가하였고, 신청자로부터의 진술 청취는 덜 포괄적으로 이루어지게 되었습니다. 이러한 조정으로 인하여 난민 심사관 및 미국 정부가 신청자의 신원이 적절하게 확인되었는지 여부를 정확하게 판단하고, 잠재적인 국가안보 또는 공공안전상의 우려를 평가하며, 신청자가 난민의 정의를 충족하는지 여부를 확인할 수 있는 능력이 제한되었습니다.

미국의 이익과 공공안전을 보호하기 위하여, 국토안보부(DHS)가 외국인이 난민의 정의를 충족하지 못하였으며 입국 당시 난민 지위를 받을 자격이 없었다고 판단하는 경우, 미국 시민권이민서비스국(USCIS)은 신속하게 조치를 취해야 합니다. NOIT(종료의향통지서) 응답 기간을 단축하면 DHS가 이러한 판단에 신속하게 대응할 수 있습니다. 통지 기간을 더 길게 허용할 경우 3 USCIS Announces Results of Operation Twin Shield, a Large-Scale Immigration Fraud Investigation (2025년 9월 30일), https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/news-releases/uscis-announces-results-of-operation- twin-shield-a-large-scale-immigration-fraud-investigation 참조

외국인이 단속을 회피하거나 유해한 활동에 가담할 기회를 제공할 수 있습니다. 예를 들어, 사기탐지 및 국가안보국(Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, FDNS)은 이후 무장단체의 구성원으로 확인되거나 극단주의 조직과의 연계를 은폐한 것으로 밝혀진 난민 사건들을 조사한 바 있습니다. 한 사건에서는 한 난민이 라이베리아 내전 당시 라이베리아 무장군과 함께 인권침해 행위에 가담한 것으로 밝혀졌습니다. 또 다른 사건에서는 한 난민이 에티오피아의 무장단체인 오로모해방전선(Oromo Liberation Front, OLF)과의 관련성을 허위로 진술한 것으로 밝혀졌습니다. 소셜미디어 조사 결과, 그가 미국에 난민으로 입국하기 전에 다수의 친OLF 활동과 친OLF 및 급진적 폭력 선동 발언을 게시한 것으로 확인되었습니다. 이러한 사건들은 난민의 입국 이후 국가안보 또는 공공안전에 관한 신빙성 있는 증거가 발견되는 경우, USCIS가 종료 절차가 완료될 때까지 추방 절차를 개시하지 못할 수 있음을 보여줍니다. 따라서 NOIT 발급 이후 응답 기간을 10일로 단축하면 USCIS가 이러한 위협에 더욱 신속하고 효과적으로 대응하여 이민제도의 건전성을 회복할 수 있습니다.

난민으로서 미국에 입국할 자격을 갖추기 위하여, 외국인은 무엇보다도 이민국적법(INA) 제101(a)(42)(A) 및 (B)호, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) 및 (B)에 정의된 "난민"의 정의를 충족함을 입증하여야 하며, 이는 박해자가 아니어야 한다는 요건을 포함합니다. USCIS가 외국인의 미국 입국 이후, 해당 외국인이 입국 당시 난민의 정의를 충족하지 못하였고 따라서 난민 분류를 위한 자격 요건을 충족하지 못하여 입국이 허용되지 말았어야 했다는 사실을 발견한 경우, 법적으로 가능한 모든 조치를 취함으로써, 즉 법적 근거가 있는 경우 해당 외국인을 가능한 한 신속하게 미국에서 추방하는 것을 포함하여, 미국 이민제도의 건전성을 보호하는 것이 중요합니다. 외국인의 신원이 완전히 확인되지 않은 경우에는 국가안보 및 공공안전에 내재적인 위험이 존재합니다. 따라서 적절한 경우 난민 지위 종료 절차를 간소화할 수 있는 능력은 미국 국민의 안전과 합법적인 미국 이민제도의 건전성에 즉각적으로 기여합니다.

외국인이 입국 당시 난민이 아니었다고 판단되는 경우 난민 지위를 종료하기 위한 현행 통지 및 응답 절차는 비효율적이며 미국의 안보와 안전을 저해합니다. NOIT에 대한 응답 기간을 10일이 아닌 30일로 제공하는 것은 자격이 없는 외국인이 받을 자격이 없는 이민 혜택을 더 오랫동안 유지할 수 있도록 하여 미국 이민제도의 건전성과 미국의 국익을 훼손합니다. 더욱이 외국인이 받을 자격이 없는 지위를 유지하면서 동시에 그의 진정한 신원에 관한 정보가 불충분하여 적절히 심사받지 못한 경우, 미국 사회의 안전과 보안에 위험이 발생합니다.

B. 법적 권한
국토안보부(DHS) 장관(이하 "장관")이 본 임시최종규칙(IFR)에서 이루어진 규정 개정에 대하여 가지는 권한은 이민국적법(INA), 8 U.S.C. 1101 이하, 그리고 2002년 국토안보법(HSA), Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135(일부는 6 U.S.C. 101 이하에 성문화됨)의 여러 조항에서 찾을 수 있습니다. INA에 따라 장관은 난민의 입국, 지위 종료, 추방 및 지위 조정에 관한 권한을 가집니다. 예를 들어 INA 제207조, 제209조, 8 U.S.C. 1157, 1159를 참조하십시오.4 가장 중요한 것은, INA 제207(c)(4)조, 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4)는 장관이 외국인이 "입국 당시 실제로 난민이 아니었다"고 판단하는 경우 해당 외국인 및 그 배우자 또는 자녀의 난민 지위를 종료할 수 있도록 허용하며, 그러한 종료의 4 또한 HSA 제451(b)(3)조 및 (5)조, 6 U.S.C. 271(b)(3), (5)(HSA 제정 이전에 이민귀화국(Immigration and Naturalization Service, "INS")이 수행하던 난민 신청 심사 및 기타 심사에 관한 권한을 DHS로 이관하는 조항)를 참조하십시오.

절차를 규율하는 규정을 발령하도록 장관에게 명시적으로 권한을 부여합니다. 장관은 난민 지위를 부여하고 그러한 지위를 조정하거나 종료할 권한을 미국 시민권이민서비스국(USCIS)에 위임하였습니다.5 본 임시최종규칙(IFR) 발령에 관한 일반적 권한은 INA 제103(a)조, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)에서 찾을 수 있으며, 이는 장관이 이민 및 국적법을 관리, 집행하고 그러한 권한을 수행하는 데 필요하다고 판단하는 규정을 수립하도록 권한을 부여합니다. 또한 HSA 제102조, 6 U.S.C. 112는 DHS의 모든 기능을 장관에게 귀속시키고 장관이 규정을 발령할 수 있도록 권한을 부여합니다.6 본 규칙에 관한 추가적인 권한은 다음에서 찾을 수 있습니다.

• HSA 제101(b)(1)(F)조, 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F)는 "국토를 보안하기 위한 노력, 활동 및 프로그램으로 인하여 미국의 전반적인 경제 안보가 저해되지 않도록 보장하는" 것을 DHS의 주요 임무로 규정합니다.
• INA 제101(a)(42)조, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)는 난민을 정의합니다.
• HSA 제451(a)(3)조, 6 U.S.C. 271(a)(3)는 USCIS 국장에게 "[이민 심사] 기능을 수행하기 위한 정책"을 수립할 권한을 부여합니다.
C. 규제 조치 개요
본 임시최종규칙(IFR)을 통해 DHS는 8 CFR 207.9를 개정하여, USCIS에 의해 난민 지위가 종료되는 외국인에 대한 통지 및 답변 기간을 30일에서 10일로 변경합니다.

D. 관련 규칙 제정
DHS는 다양한 개발 단계에 있는 여러 규칙 제정 조치를 진행하고 있습니다.7 DHS는 이들 각 규칙이 본 규칙에 미치는 주변적, 중복적 및 상호 관련된 영향에 대하여 검토하고 분석하였으며, 본 임시최종규칙(IFR)이 난민 지위 종료 절차에 한정하여 좁게 초점을 맞추고 있으므로 그러한 영향이 없음을 확인하였습니다.

DHS는 또한 가능한 범위 내에서 USCIS가 인지하고 있는 정책 변경 가능성이 있을 경우 그 영향을 고려하였습니다. 예를 들어, 2026년 2월 18일 ICE와 USCIS가 공동으로 발표한 각서는 난민 지위를 가진 개인들에게 영향을 미치는 것으로서, "이민관이 영주권 지위로 조정하지 못한 난민을 구금할 수 있는 시기 및 상황에 관한 USCIS와 ICE의 정책"을 규정하고 있습니다.8 해당 각서에서 발표된 정책 변경 사항은 난민의 조건부 입국 및 지위 조정을 규율하는 이민국적법(INA) 제209조, 8 U.S.C. 1159의 법정 요건과 관련된 것으로, 미국 내에 최소 1년 이상 거주하였으나 이민국적법 제209조(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1159(a)(1)에 따라 아직 영주권 지위를 취득하지 못한 난민에 대하여, DHS가 해당 난민을 영주권자로서의 입국 심사를 위하여 체포하고 구금할 수 있다고 규정하고 있습니다.9 이러한 정책 변경은 국가안보, 공공안전 및 사기 관련 문제에 대한 심사를 포함하여 난민으로 입국이 허가된 외국인에 대한 심사를 통해 공익을 보호하는 것을 목적으로 한다는 점에서 유사하나, 본 규칙의 초점은 지위 조정에 실패한 난민의 구금, 체포 또는 유치가 아니라 종결 사건의 절차에 있습니다.

III. 배경 및 목적 A. 최초 난민 처리 절차 미국 내 난민 지위는 그것이 부여하는 혜택 및 영주 지위로 이어지는 경로로 인하여, 전 세계 실향민들에게 매우 선호되는 이민 혜택입니다. 미국 난민입국프로그램(USRAP)을 통한 미국으로의 재정착은 여러 기관 파트너가 관여하는 다단계 절차입니다. 미국 국무부(State)는 연례 협의 절차를 주관하고, 난민 재정착 활동에 자금을 지원하고 이를 감독하며, USCIS 인터뷰 전후 지원을 제공하는 비정부기구와 계약을 체결하고, 우선순위 1(Priority 1) 사건을 USRAP 절차에 회부하는 역할을 합니다. 외국인이 USRAP에 접근할 자격이 있는 것으로 결정된 후에는, Form I-590, 난민 분류 등록 신청서(Registration for Classification as Refugee)를 제출할 수 있습니다.10 난민 분류 신청서는 주로 해외에서 접수 처리되며, USCIS 난민심사관이 해당 외국인이 난민의 정의에 부합하는지 및 그 밖에 미국 재정착 자격을 갖추었는지 여부를 심사하여 결정합니다. 미국 법률에 따라 난민 분류 자격을 갖추기 위하여 신청인은 다음 사항을 입증하여야 합니다.
•본인의 국적국 밖에 소재할 것 11 •미국에 대하여 특별한 인도적 관심의 대상일 것
•인종, 종교, 국적, 정치적 견해 또는 특정 사회집단의 구성원 신분을 이유로 박해를 받았거나 박해를 받을 것을 우려할 것
•다른 국가에 확고히 재정착하지 아니하였을 것, 그리고 •미국으로의 이민자로서 입국 허용 대상일 것

이민국적법(INA) 제101조(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42) 및 이민국적법 제207조(c)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(1) 참조. 난민에는 인종, 종교, 국적, 특정 사회집단의 구성원 신분 또는 정치적 견해를 이유로 타인에 대한 박해를 명령하거나 선동하거나 지원하거나 그 밖에 이에 가담한 자는 포함되지 아니합니다. 위와 동일.

USCIS 심사관은 위의 자격 요건을 기초로 난민 분류 자격 여부를 판정합니다. USCIS가 난민 분류 신청을 승인하면, 미국 세관국경보호청(CBP)은 해당 승인일로부터 4개월 이내에 미국 입국항에 도착하는 외국인을 난민으로서 “조건부로” 입국시킬 권한을 부여받습니다.12 미국 보건복지부 산하 난민정착국은 미국에 난민으로 입국이 허가된 외국인에게 취업 훈련, 영어 교육, 현금 지원(조기 자립을 도모하는 방식으로 제공됨) 및 취업 알선을 포함한 정착 지원을 제공합니다. 주신청 난민의 동반가족에는 주신청 난민의 배우자 및 21세 미만의 미혼 자녀가 포함될 수 있습니다.13 동반가족은 최초 난민 지위 신청에 포함되거나 주신청 난민이 미국에 도착한 이후에 별도로 청원될 수 있습니다. 위와 같음. 동반가족이 난민으로서 미국에 입국하기 위해서는 입국 적격성을 갖추고 박해자 제외 사유에 해당하지 않음을 입증하여야 하나, 과거 박해 경험이나 장래 박해에 대한 충분한 근거 있는 공포와 같은 난민 정의 또는 그 요건을 충족한다는 점을 입증할 필요는 없습니다.
미국 내 정착 지원 외에도, 난민은 미국 도착 즉시 취업 허가를 받습니다.14 12 8 CFR 207.4(난민 분류가 승인된 외국인을 입국시킬 수 있는 CBP의 권한). 13 INA 제207조(c)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(2).

B. 난민 지위의 종료 USCIS가 난민으로서 미국에 조건부로 입국이 허가된 외국인의 지위를 종료할 수 있는 유일한 근거는, USCIS가 해당 외국인이 미국 입국 당시 난민의 정의를 충족하지 못하였다고 판단하는 경우입니다.15 법률상 그 밖의 다른 종료 사유는 규정되어 있지 않습니다. 입국 당시 실제로 난민 정의를 충족하지 못한 외국인은 입국 부적격 사유에 해당하였을 것이며, 그 지위가 종료된 이후에는 일반적으로 미국에 체류할 법적 근거를 상실하게 됩니다.16 입국 당시 난민 정의를 충족하지 못하였다는 이유로 난민 지위를 종료하는 판정은 오로지 주신청 난민에게만 적용되며, 동반 난민에게는 적용되지 않습니다. 난민 지위를 인정받기 위해서는, 주신청자는 INA 제101조(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)에 규정된 난민 정의의 요건을 충족하여야 하고, 미국 입국에 적격하여야 하며, 지정된 미국 난민수용프로그램(USRAP) 처리 우선순위 중 하나에 해당하여야 합니다.17 USCIS는 주신청 난민의 지위가 종료되는 경우 이에 따라 동반 난민의 지위도 종료할 수 있습니다.18 난민 지위는 해당 외국인이 난민 지위를 유지하고 있고 아직 합법적 영주권자(LPR) 지위로 조정되거나 귀화하지 아니한 경우에 한하여 종료될 수 있습니다.19 다만, USCIS가 INA 제246조, 8 U.S.C. 1156에 따라 외국인의 LPR 지위를 취소한 경우, 난민으로 입국이 허가되었던 외국인은 이전의 난민 지위로 환원되며, 종료 사유가 법정 요건을 충족하는 경우 그 난민 지위는 종료될 수 있습니다.20 15 INA 제207조(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4).

16 8 CFR 207.9 참조(USCIS가 입국 당시 외국인이 INA 제101조(a)(42)의 의미 내에서 “난민이 아니었다”고 판단하는 경우에 한하여 난민 지위의 종료를 허용함), INA 제237조(a)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(1)(A)(“입국 당시” 입국 부적격 사유가 있었던 비시민권자를 강제퇴거 대상으로 규정함), 이는 그 밖에 INA 제212조(a)(7)(A)(i)(I), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(7)(A)(i)(I)(유효한 이민 입국서류의 결여로 인한 입국 부적격)을 포함함.

18 8 CFR 207.7(d) 및 207.9 참조, 또한 "모든 외국인(및 그 배우자 또는 자녀)의 난민 지위는 종료될 수 있다"고 규정하는 INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4)도 참조(강조 추가). 19 Matter of D-K-, 25 I&N Dec. 761 (BIA 2012); Matter of Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836 (BIA 2005). 20 미국 시민권이민서비스국(USCIS) 정책 매뉴얼, 제7권, Q편, 합법적 영주권의 취소, https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-7-part-q (2026년 1월 22일 마지막 방문). USCIS가 주된 난민이 입국 당시 INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)에 정의된 난민에 해당하지 않았다고 판단하는 경우, USCIS는 난민 지위의 종료 절차를 개시합니다. 구 이민귀화국(INS)은 1980년 난민법(Refugee Act of 1980) 제정에 따라 난민 지위 종료를 규율하는 규정을 처음으로 시행하였으며, 이후 45년 동안 그 절차는 실질적으로 변경되지 않았습니다.21 USCIS는 종료 이전에 종료 의향 통지서(Notice of Intent to Terminate, NOIT)를 발급합니다.22 NOIT에서 USCIS는 외국인이 경험하였거나 우려한 피해가 보호 사유에 기인하지 않았다는 USCIS의 판단 또는 예를 들어 외국인이 다른 국적이나 다른 국가의 법적 지위를 보유하고 있어 주장한 국가 출신의 난민으로 인정될 자격이 없다는 사실 등 종료의 구체적인 근거를 명시합니다. NOIT는 또한 외국인에게 자신의 난민 주장을 뒷받침하고 제안된 종료에 반대하는 서면 또는 구두 증거를 제출할 권리가 있음을 고지합니다. 이번 임시최종규칙(IFR) 이전에는 8 CFR 207.9에 따라 외국인에게 NOIT에 대응할 30일의 기간이 부여되었습니다. 이 절차를 시행한 전문(preamble)에는 (다른 더 짧거나 더 긴 기간이 아닌) 30일의 응답 기간에 대한 이민귀화국(INS)의 근거가 설명되어 있지 않았습니다.23 외국인이 구두 증언을 제공하기로 선택하는 경우, USCIS가 통지서 발급일로부터 30일 이내에 면접을 일정화할 수 있도록 추가 면접 요청 사실을 USCIS에 통보하여야 합니다. 외국인은 또한 통지서 상단에 기재된 반신 주소로 통지서 발급일로부터 30일 이내에 서류 증거를 제출할 수 있습니다. 21 45 FR 37392 (1980년 6월 2일) (임시최종규칙), 46 FR 45116 (1981년 9월 10일) (최종규칙). INS와 국토안보부(DHS)는 8 CFR 207.9가 최초로 공표된 이후 최소한의 변경만을 가하였습니다. 불법이민개혁 및 이민자책임법(IIRIRA) 제정 이후, INS는 난민 지위 종료 후 적용될 수 있는 추방 절차의 유형에 관한 참조 조항을 갱신하였습니다. Inspection and Expedited Removal of Aliens; Detention and Removal of Aliens; Conduct of Removal Proceedings; Asylum Procedures, 62 FR 10312, 10337 (1997년 3월 6일)도 참조. 그 밖의 경미한 변경으로는 207.8에서 207.9로의 번호 재조정 및 갱신된 DHS 송달 절차의 포함이 있었습니다. Procedures for Filing a Derivative Petition (Form I-730) for a Spouse and Unmarried Children of a Refugee/Asylee, 63 FR 3792 (1998년 1월 27일); Immigration Benefits Business Transformation, Increment I, 76 FR 53764, 53784 (2011년 8월 29일).
통지서.24 NOIT는 정해진 기간 내에 통지서에 응답하지 않는 경우 외국인의 난민 지위가 종료된다는 점을 명확히 밝힙니다.
마지막으로, NOIT는 USCIS가 외국인이 입국 당시 INA 제101조(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)의 의미 내에서 난민에 해당하지 않았다고 판단하는 경우, 그의 난민 지위 및 취업허가가 종료되며 미국으로부터 추방 대상이 됨을 명시합니다.
DHS는 통상적으로 외국인의 영주권으로의 신분 조정에 대한 최종 심사 이전에 그 기초가 되는 난민 판정을 검토하며, 정당한 사유가 있는 경우 종료 절차를 개시합니다. 다만, DHS가 외국인이 난민으로 입국할 당시 난민 지위에 대한 자격이 없었다고 판단하는 경우, 신분 조정 이전 어느 시점에서도 종료 절차가 개시될 수 있습니다.

USCIS(미국 시민권이민서비스국)의 난민 지위 종료 결정에 대하여는 항소할 수 없습니다.25 지위가 종료되면 USCIS는 이민국적법(INA) 제235조, 제240조 및 제241조에 따라 해당 외국인에 대한 추방 절차를 진행합니다.26 USCIS는 또한 난민으로 입국이 허가된 자를, 난민 지위를 종료하지 아니하고도, 신분조정 신청서에 대한 심사 없이 적용 가능한 추방 사유에 근거하여 직접 추방 절차에 회부할 수 있습니다.27 C. 오류가 있는 난민 입국의 위험을 증가시킨 전 행정부의 조치 매년 대통령은 1980년 난민법(Refugee Act of 1980)에 의해 마련된 난민 수용 상한선을 설정합니다.
